1.title: Monitoring, Logs and Debugging
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Monitoring, Logs and Debugging. It covers the exam area Application Observability and Maintenance. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Use built-in C L I tools to monitor Kubernetes applications. Utilize container logs. Debugging in Kubernetes. Practice with seven hands-on labs worth forty-one points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Observability and Maintenance (fifteen percent). Practice in this module: seven labs, forty-one points, about forty-four minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: A debugging routine that works every time
1.text: A debugging routine that works every time. The figure shows this: From status to cause. Exam tip: Run kube control describe pod and read the Events at the end first: they usually name the cause.

1.title: A debugging routine that works every time, continued
1.text: A debugging routine that works every time. Start with the status, and let it tell you where to look. Do these in order and stop when you find the cause. one. Status. Command: kube control get pods dash o wide. What it tells you: the status word, ready, restarts, the node. two. Events. Command: kube control describe pod pod (read the Events at the bottom). What it tells you: why scheduling, pulling or starting failed. three. Logs. Command: kube control logs pod ( dash c, the previous flag ). What it tells you: what the app itself said.

1.title: A debugging routine that works every time, continued
1.text: A debugging routine that works every time. four. Inside. Command: kube control exec -it pod then the command sh. What it tells you: the app's view: files, D N S, network. five. Cluster events. Command: kube control get events the sort by flag set to dot last Timestamp. What it tells you: the newest events of the namespace.

1.title: What the status word tells you
1.text: What the status word tells you. Pending. Usual cause: no node fits (C P U or memory request too big, taint, unbound P V C (Persistent Volume Claim), unmatched node selector). Where to look: describe Events: "zero or three nodes are available...". Container Creating (long). Usual cause: volume or secret problem, slow image pull. Where to look: describe. err image pull, image pull back off. Usual cause: wrong image name or tag, private registry without a pull secret. Where to look: describe. create container config error. Usual cause: a referenced Config Map, Secret or key does not exist. Where to look: describe. crash loop back off. Usual cause: the process exits with an error again and again. Where to look: logs the previous flag. Error or O O M killed. Usual cause: exit code not zero or memory limit exceeded. Where to look: describe (Last State), logs. Init zero slash one, Init Error. Usual cause: an init container is not finished. Where to look: logs dash c init container. Running but zero slash one Ready. Usual cause: readiness probe failing. Where to look: describe, get endpoints. Terminating for ever. Usual cause: finalizer or a stuck volume. Where to look: describe; last resort delete the force flag the grace period flag set to zero.

1.title: Container logs
1.text: Container logs. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: After a restart use kube control logs the previous flag, and with several containers always name one with dash c.

1.title: Container logs, continued
1.text: Container logs. Logs are what the container wrote to standard output and standard error. An app that writes to a file inside the container (not to stdout) has no kube control logs: read the file with exec, or add a sidecar that tails it (Module three). Logs of a deleted Pod are gone; a crashed container's previous log is kept only for the last restart.

1.title: Container logs, continued
1.text: Container logs. Save logs to a file on the exam host with the shell redirect: kube control logs web dash c worker the tail flag set to three about slash answers slash worker tail dot txt. kube control logs prints a "Defaulted container..." note to stderr when a Pod has several containers and you did not choose one, and it then reads the first container: read the task carefully for the container name.

1.title: Resource usage: kubectl top
1.text: Resource usage: kube control top. kube control top needs the Metrics Server (installed on the cluster; if top says "Metrics A P I not available", it is missing or still starting). The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: kube control top needs the Metrics Server and shows actual use, not requests or limits.

1.title: Resource usage: kubectl top, continued
1.text: Resource usage: kube control top. C P U is in millicores ( two hundred fifty millicores is a quarter of a core); memory is in Mi. The numbers are a recent average and take about a minute to appear for a new Pod. They show use, not the requests or limits you set (those are in describe ).

1.title: Getting inside and moving data
1.text: Getting inside and moving data. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Getting inside and moving data, continued
1.text: Getting inside and moving data. Ephemeral debug containers. Many images have no shell ( distroless, pause ). You cannot exec into them, and a Pod's containers cannot be added after creation. kube control debug attaches a temporary container with the tools you want to a running Pod, sharing its network and, with the target flag, its process space. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Getting inside and moving data, continued
1.text: Getting inside and moving data. An ephemeral container is listed in spec dot ephemeral Containers, is not restarted, and cannot be removed; delete the Pod when you are done. Exam tip: kube control debug attaches a temporary container to a Pod whose image has no shell.

1.title: Typical faults and the fix
1.text: Typical faults and the fix. crash loop back off, log says a setting is missing. add the env, Config Map or Secret the log names ( kube control set env deployment app key value ). create container config error for a Config Map. create the Config Map with the exact name and key that describe shows. image pull back off. correct the image name or tag: kube control set image deployment web engine X engine X alpine. Pending: "Insufficient cpu". lower the request (Pod: delete and recreate; Deployment: edit). Pods zero slash one Ready. fix the readiness probe path or port, or the app. Service without endpoints. the Service selector must match the Pod labels (Module fourteen).

1.title: Typical faults and the fix, continued
1.text: Typical faults and the fix. Exam tip. Do not guess: run kube control describe pod and read the last five lines. The Events almost always name the cause. Then change one thing and verify. Exam tip. A Deployment's Pods are replaced when you change the template, so edit the Deployment. A bare Pod's resources, image pull policy and most spec fields cannot be edited: export the yamel, change it, delete and recreate.

1.title: Lab 8.1: logs one container
1.text: Lab eight point one: logs one container. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Pod shop in the namespace dbg has two containers, web and worker. Write only the last three lines of the log of the container worker to about slash answers slash worker tail dot txt on the host where you run kube control. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 8.1: logs one container, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg logs shop dash c worker the tail flag set to three about slash answers slash worker tail dot txt. Then cat about slash answers slash worker tail dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.title: Lab 8.2: crashloop env
1.text: Lab eight point two: crashloop env. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace dbg, the Pod of the Deployment app keeps crashing ( crash loop back off ). Read the container log to find the cause and fix it without changing the image or the command: the application needs the environment variable D B U R L with the value postgres or or db five thousand four hundred thirty-two slash app. Wait until the Deployment has one Ready replica. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 8.2: crashloop env, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg get pods. Then kube control dash n dbg logs deploy slash app the tail flag set to five. Then kube control dash n dbg set env deployment app D B U R L postgres or or db five thousand four hundred thirty-two slash app. Then kube control dash n dbg rollout status deployment app the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 8.3: top pods
2.text: Lab eight point three: top pods. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace load, three Pods are running and the cluster has the Metrics Server. Find the Pod that uses the most C P U right now with kube control top and write only its name to about slash answers slash top dot txt on the host where you run kube control. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 8.3: top pods, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n load top pods. Then kube control dash n load top pods the sort by flag set to cpu the no headers flag head -one awk print one about slash answers slash top dot txt. Then cat about slash answers slash top dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 8.4: ephemeral debug container
2.text: Lab eight point four: ephemeral debug container. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Pod tiny in the namespace dbg runs an image that has no shell, so you cannot exec into it. Without recreating the Pod, attach an ephemeral debug container named dbg (image busy box one dot thirty-six, targeting the container tiny ) that runs sh dash c echo debug ok slash temp slash dbg dot txt sleep three thousand six hundred. The Pod must stay Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 8.4: ephemeral debug container, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg debug tiny the image flag set to busy box one dot thirty-six the target flag set to tiny the container flag set to dbg then the command sh dash, and so on. Then for i in seq one thirty do kube control dash n dbg get pod tiny dash o json path dot status dot ephemeral Container Statuses zero dot state dot running grep dash q started, and so on. Then kube control dash n dbg exec tiny dash c dbg then the command cat slash temp slash dbg dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 8.5: exec read files
2.text: Lab eight point five: exec read files. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Pod files in the namespace dbg runs a container named main. Without changing the Pod: write the content of the file slash E T C slash app slash version inside the container (just the text) to about slash answers slash version dot txt, and write the number of lines of the file slash var slash log slash app dot log inside the container (just the number) to about slash answers slash lines dot txt, both on the host where you run kube control. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 8.5: exec read files, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg exec files dash c main then the command cat slash E T C slash app slash version about slash answers slash version dot txt. Then kube control dash n dbg exec files dash c main then the command wc dash l slash var slash log slash app dot log awk print one about slash answers slash lines dot txt. Then cat about slash answers slash version dot txt about slash answers slash lines dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 8.6: fix pending pod
2.text: Lab eight point six: fix pending pod. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Pod big in the namespace dbg (manifest about slash work slash big dot yaml ) stays Pending. Find the reason in its events and fix the manifest so that the Pod is Running: lower the C P U request to one hundred millicores. Keep the name, image and namespace. A Pod's resources cannot be edited in place, so recreate it. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 8.6: fix pending pod, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg describe pod big then pipe to tail -five. Then kube control dash n dbg delete pod big the wait flag set to true. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then kube control apply dash f about slash work slash big dot yaml. Then kube control dash n dbg wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash big the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 8.7: missing configmap
2.text: Lab eight point seven: missing configmap. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace dbg, the Pod of the Deployment svc does not start ( create container config error ). Find the cause with kube control describe, and fix it without changing the Deployment: create what is missing so that the Deployment has one Ready replica. The application expects level info from that source. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 8.7: missing configmap, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n dbg describe pod dash l app svc then pipe to grep dash i -A three Events. Then kube control dash n dbg create configmap app config the from literal flag set to level info. Then kube control dash n dbg rollout status deployment svc the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which command shows the log of the previous container instance? Answer: kube control logs pod the previous flag. Question two. How do you read the log of one container of a multi-container Pod? Answer: kube control logs pod dash c container. Question three. What does Running with zero slash one ready mean? Answer: The container runs but its readiness probe fails (or the app is not ready).

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which component must exist for kube control top to work? Answer: The Metrics Server. Question five. How do you list Pods by memory use, the largest first? Answer: kube control top pods the sort by flag set to memory. Question six. Which command attaches a temporary tools container to a running Pod? Answer: kube control debug pod the image flag set to image the target flag set to container.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. What does create container config error usually mean? Answer: A Config Map, Secret or key that the Pod references does not exist. Question eight. Where do you read why a Pod is Pending? Answer: In the Events at the end of kube control describe pod.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Routine: get (status), describe (events), logs ( dash c, the previous flag ), exec. Logs: stdout and stderr only; the tail flag, the since flag, dash f, dash l, the all containers flag. top: Metrics Server; the sort by flag set to cpu memory, the containers flag; millicores and Mi. debug: ephemeral container ( the target flag ), the copy to flag, node or name. Data: exec... file, cp, port forward. Statuses: Pending, image pull back off, create container config error, crash loop back off, zero slash one Ready. Fix location: Deployment: edit it; bare Pod: delete and recreate.
